body: Your campus is funded. The permits are approved. The hardware is on order. But one obstacle is standing between you and operations: the grid connection queue -- and it could keep you waiting for years while competitors come online.

This isn't a niche problem. The International Energy Agency estimates that approximately 20% of planned global data center projects face significant delays due to power access constraints, with interconnection wait times reaching up to a decade in some markets.
In Northern Virginia, the world's largest data center market, the average wait is
up to seven years.

The AI infrastructure buildout cannot wait that long. And the operators getting online fastest in 2026 aren't waiting for the grid to catch up, they're changing what the grid sees when it evaluates their facility.
What the Interconnection Queue Actually Is
Before a data center can draw power from the grid, it must go through an interconnection study process,
essentially a queue for grid access approvals.
The process was designed for an era of smaller, more predictable load growth. It was not designed for 300-megawatt AI campuses that need power on competitive timescales.
Here's what happens inside the queue:     Impact study:
The utility evaluates how your facility affects the broader grid

under worst-case scenarios (peak system demand, major equipment outages, and your facility running at full load simultaneously).     Facilities study: If the impact study identifies required upgrades, a facilities study determines exactly what infrastructure needs to be built and at what cost.     Interconnection agreement: Once studies are complete and costs are assigned, a formal agreement is negotiated -- often a multi-year process in itself.
Construction and energization: The physical infrastructure is built, inspections are completed, and the facility is
energized.
Compounding this:
the queue operates on a roughly first-come, first-served basis.

Speculative facilities (projects that aren't yet ready to build) have historically been allowed to occupy queue positions ahead of those that are ready, creating backlogs that delay legitimate projects by years.
How Long Are We Actually Talking?
The timelines vary by market, but
nowhere in the US is the standard interconnection process fast enough for competitive AI infrastructure development.

Data Center Grid Connection Timeline: Standard vs. With BTM Battery (Time from site selection to energization -- US major markets)     Northern Virginia (PJM): 84 mo / 7 yrs     California (CAISO): 66 mo / 5 yrs 6 mo     Texas (ERCOT): 60 mo / 5 yrs     Midwest (MISO): 60 mo / 5 yrs     Average -- no battery: 66 mo / 5 yrs 6 mo     Average -- with BTM battery: 21 mo / 1 yr 9 mo     Sources: Latitude Media, IEA, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Verse analysis.
In Northern Virginia, still considered the global capital of data center development, average wait times in the interconnection queue have reached seven years.
Texas (ERCOT) and the Midwest (MISO) run closer to five years. California (CAISO) sits around five and a half.
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory research confirms that interconnection wait times have more than doubled over the past fifteen years. The trajectory is not improving on its own.

The competitive math is brutal. If your competitor breaks ground on their interconnection application today and you start in six months, under the standard process they could be generating revenue from AI workloads three to four years before you reach full operations. That gap compounds every quarter.
Why the Standard Workarounds Don't Solve It
Most existing advice about the interconnection queue falls into one of four categories. Each has real limitations.
Wait it out --

Competitors aren't waiting. Every quarter in the queue is a quarter of AI infrastructure capacity advantage handed to whoever is already online. Patience is not a strategy in a market where hyperscalers are racing to deploy compute at scale.

Site selection in less-constrained markets -- The markets with the fastest interconnection timelines are typically the markets with the least demand, and the least access to fiber, talent, customers, and cloud on-ramps. The constrained markets are constrained because that's where the demand is.
Wait for policy change --
Regulatory reform of the interconnection process is underway across multiple ISOs and FERC. It matters. But
it operates on decade timescales, not campus timescales.
Individual projects cannot wait for system-wide reform.

Buy powered land -- Powered land transactions (parcels with confirmed power capacity and delivery timelines) have become a significant market segment. Transactions in the 250-500MW range have become standard as developers recognize that land without power capacity cannot support competitive development timelines. But supply is finite, prices reflect the scarcity, and the market for powered sites in major markets is intensely competitive.
